title: Create a Fabric data agent - Microsoft Fabric | Microsoft Learn
summary: Microsoft Learn's how-to for building a Fabric data agent end to end: creating the item, attaching data sources, configuring agent-level and data-source-level instructions plus few-shot example queries, testing the chat experience, and publishing/sharing a draft-vs-published version with colleagues.
audience: Builders and platform teams standing up their first data agent, plus architects who need to know the prerequisite capacity/tenant settings and the exact permission model before scoping a rollout.
why_it_matters: The mechanics of how a question becomes a prompt (schema fetch under user credentials, plus instructions/examples, then tool selection) explain why data agent output quality is really a configuration and content-curation problem, not a model problem, and the capacity/tenant/permission prerequisites determine whether a team can even turn the feature on.
takeaways: A data agent needs a paid F2+ (or P1+) capacity plus an explicit tenant-level cross-geo AI setting turned on before it can be used at all.

No customer-supplied Azure OpenAI key is needed — Fabric brokers a Microsoft-managed Azure OpenAI Assistant, but schema/query execution still runs under the asking user's own Entra ID identity and permissions.
Quality tuning happens through two independent instruction layers (agent-level and per-data-source) plus few-shot example queries, not through any model fine-tuning.
Publishing keeps draft and published versions separate, so an author can keep iterating without disrupting colleagues already querying the shared version.
Workspace outbound access protection, when enabled, can silently break agent queries to external data sources unless admins allowlist the connection.

claims.text: Creating or evaluating a Fabric data agent requires a paid F2-or-higher Fabric capacity, or a Power BI Premium P1-or-higher capacity with Fabric enabled, as the baseline capacity prerequisite.
Before a data agent can run, an admin must separately enable cross-geo processing and cross-geo storing for AI at the tenant level, a distinct switch from simply having capacity.
No customer-managed Azure OpenAI key or access token is required to use a data agent; Fabric brokers a Microsoft-managed Azure OpenAI Assistant and handles that authentication internally.

When Workspace outbound access protection is enabled on the workspace, a data agent's calls to external data sources are governed by the workspace's data connection rules, but the Microsoft-managed Azure OpenAI service the agent relies on is exempt from that protection.

When answering a question, the agent first fetches the target data source's schema using the requesting user's own credentials, guaranteeing schema visibility is scoped to what that user can already see.

The prompt sent to the underlying Azure OpenAI Assistant is assembled from three inputs: the user's natural-language question, the fetched schema metadata, and any creator-supplied instructions or example queries, before the assistant selects a query-generation tool.

A data agent can attach up to five data sources in any combination of lakehouses, warehouses, Power BI semantic models, KQL databases, ontologies, and Microsoft Graph, including tables exposed only through OneLake shortcuts, queried without copying data.

Agent-level instructions accept up to 15,000 characters of plain-English guidance and can direct the agent to prefer specific sources for specific question types or define domain-specific terminology the model otherwise misinterprets.

Example queries function as few-shot learning: creators pair sample questions with validated SQL or KQL, and the agent matches new questions against these to steer generation toward business-specific logic; only syntactically valid, schema-matching examples are ever used, and Power BI semantic models don't support this example-query mechanism.

Publishing a data agent creates two independent versions — an editable draft and a separately shareable published copy — so an author can keep refining the draft without disrupting colleagues already querying the published version.

When a workspace shares OneLake data from another tenant via external data sharing, a data agent can query that shared data through the shortcut created at share acceptance, with the consumer tenant's governance policies applying and no additional authentication configuration needed.

Consumers who only query a shared data agent backed by Power BI semantic models need Read permission on those models and do not need workspace-level access at all; Write permission is required only to modify the model or use Prep for AI.
